subject: Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape

messages.author: 4b6a033bb73e401c
messages.subject: Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape
parts:
Hi all

I'm trying to fit a beta distribution where the mean and total count parameters depend on covariates:

phi_i ~ normal(0, 1)
phi_j ~ normal(0, 10)
phi_ij <- inv_logit(phi_i + phi_j)

lambda_i ~ normal(0, 1)
lambda_j ~ normal(0, 10)
lambda _ij <- exp(lambda_i + lambda_j)

a_ij <- phi_ij * lambda_ij
b_ij <- (1 - phi_ij) * lambda_ij

theta_ij ~ beta(a_ij, b_ij)

However this model occasionally infers a u-shaped beta distribution, which is unrealistic for our application.
Is there a sensible way to use the mean parameterization while constraining b_ij > 1?

-Sam

messages.author: 4b6a033bb73e401c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape
parts:
Hi Daniel, the model is below

data {
    int<lower=1> N;
    int<lower=1> R;
    int<lower=1> C;
  
    int<lower=1,upper=R> r[N];
    int<lower=1,upper=C> c[N];
      
    vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] y;
}

parameters {    
    // hyperparameters
    real<lower=0> phi_c_sigma;
    real<lower=0> lambda_c_sigma;

    vector[R] phi_r;
    vector[R] lambda_r;
    vector[C] phi_c;
    vector[C] lambda_c;
}

model {  
    vector[N] phi;
    vector[N] lambda;
    vector[N] a;
    vector[N] b;

    // hyperpriors
    phi_c_sigma ~ normal(0, 1);
    lambda_c_sigma ~ normal(0, 1);

    // priors
    phi_r ~ normal(0, 1);
    phi_c ~ normal(0, phi_c_sigma);
    lambda_r ~ normal(0, 1);
    lambda_c ~ normal(0, lambda_c_sigma);
       
    for (i in 1:N) {        

        phi[i] <- inv_logit(phi_r[r[i]] + phi_c[c[i]]);
        lambda[i] <- exp(lambda_r[r[i]] + lambda_c[c[i]]);
              
        a[i] <- lambda[i] * phi[i];
        b[i] <- lambda[i] * (1 - phi[i]);
                               
        y[i] ~ beta(a[i], b[i]);
    }
}


-Sam

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape
parts:
Since b is a function of other parameters you'd have to ensure that whatever is assigned to b satisfies that constraint. If it's not logically impossible for b to be less than 1, just highly unlikely then you'd want the priors on the primitive parameters to be such that the expression creating b is highly likely to be greater than 1.

Also, you can vectorize the call to beta() by creating a and b vectors in the loop but calling y ~ beta(a,b) outside the loop, which will be faster.

Jonah

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape
parts:
Aside from it being a bad idea statistically and computationally,
you could just set:

a[i] <- 1 + lambda[i] * phi[i];

b[i] <- 1 + lambda[i] * (1 - phi[i]);

That's a different model, though.

If you literally wanted to manage the constraints, you'd
have to set the lower bound for lambda[i] to be

max(1 / phi[i], 1 / (1 - phi[i]))

Stan won't let you express that directly, but if you
add your own Jacobians, the transforms are easy.

The reason it's a bad idea statistically is that if the data support
values for a and b less than 1, you probably don't want to rule it
out a priori --- truncating will also lead to a positive bias in
posterior means for a and b (relative to the untruncated model).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Parameterizing a beta distribution while constraining its shape
parts:
If there's substantial probability mass below 1 for
a and b with lower bounds set to 0, then you'll have
problems. Suppose you take a_raw and b_raw and set
those with lower bounds of zero and then set

a <- a_raw + 1
b <- b_raw + 1

Then the posterior is going to have a lot of mass near
zero for a_raw and b_raw, which can be unstable numerically
(in practice, this can mean underflow or very small step sizes
or some combination of both).

- Bob
